Since then kernels added mitigations on every entry and exit for CPU vulnerabilities: you can see `SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3` (separate kernel page tables) and `IBRS_ENTER` (IBRS, Indirect Branch Restricted Speculation, limits branch speculation) in today's `entry_SYSCALL_64`. Measure on your own machine before quoting a number.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it
md: The kernel's view of your memory is a list of VMAs. `execve` and ld.so create the first ones, `mmap` adds, `munmap` removes and splits, `mprotect` splits by permission, and `mremap` resizes or moves. `/proc/PID/maps` is that list, and it is the first thing to read when a mapping misbehaves.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
md: With fan-out N, the user-visible tail is set by roughly the 1 - 1/(100N) quantile of each component, not by its p99. A quantile is a percentile written as a fraction: the 0.99 quantile is p99. The formula is the N p at most 0.01 rule from the prediction, solved for p: each leaf may be slow at most 1/(100N) of the time. The wider the fan-out, the deeper into the tail you must measure and engineer.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Diameter in 4G roaming: the same trust model on IP
md: Moving from SS7 to Diameter, or to any IP protocol, does not add authentication by itself. If the edge does not check which peer may speak for which subscribers, the new protocol inherits the old trust model.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Satellite links: segments, footprints and cleartext GEO traffic
md: Link-layer encryption that silently turns off is worse than none you knew about. Put the protection you rely on at a layer you control and can monitor, such as IPsec or TLS between your own endpoints.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Merging overlapping roles: union, gaps and double counting
md: Total experience is the length of the union of role intervals, not the sum of their lengths. Sort by start, sweep, extend with max of the ends, and record gaps as you close blocks.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Verifiers set the ceiling: error rates, GenRM and self-verification
md: The false positive rate sets the ceiling, and it is multiplied by the number of wrong samples. At $p = 0.01$, even $t = 0.9$ and $f = 0.01$ give a ceiling of $0.009 / (0.009 + 0.0099) = 0.48$. Rare correct answers drown among rare false accepts: that is lesson 3's plateau, now as a formula.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model
md: Test-time compute is a second scaling axis, not a replacement for the first. It pays most when the model can already sometimes solve the task and something can recognize a correct answer.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Large-chunk TTT, one map of the design space, and the costs
md: Common failure modes: (1) Wall-clock, not FLOPs, is the bottleneck. The TTT paper reports that TTT-MLP still faces challenges in memory I/O, and Titans' throughput falls roughly linearly with memory depth. (2) Inner learning rates that are too large make the memory diverge (lesson 2). (3) Without forgetting, a fixed-size memory overflows on long inputs. (4) Most published comparisons use models under 1.5B parameters.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: What threat hunting is, and the hunt that started at 75 cents
md: A hunt assumes the attacker is already inside and that existing alerts missed them, then tests that assumption against data. Its value is not only intrusions found: like Stoll's alarms on stolen account names, what a hunt learns should become a detection, a fix, or a request for better data.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: What threat intelligence is, and what it is for
md: A feed is not intelligence. 40,000 addresses with no dates, sources, context or relevance to you are data, and a lot of it is stale or shared infrastructure (recall the shared-IP and reputation-lag traps from the alert triage course). Buying more data does not produce more intelligence; analysis against a question does.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: STIX 2.1: threat intelligence as a graph
md: STIX makes sharing easy, including sharing mistakes. A wrong `attributed-to` edge, or an indicator without `valid_until` and confidence, propagates to every consumer automatically. Model uncertainty explicitly: use confidence, Opinion objects, and leave edges out when evidence is missing.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: STRIDE: six ways things go wrong
md: Each STRIDE letter names a broken property, and the property tells you the family of fix: spoofing needs authentication, tampering needs integrity checks, repudiation needs trustworthy logs, disclosure needs confidentiality controls, denial of service needs capacity and limits, elevation needs authorization.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Defence in depth and zero trust
md: Zero trust is not a product and does not mean trusting nothing. It means no trust from network location alone. You still trust identity providers, device management and the policy engine, so those become the crown jewels and need the strongest protection.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Naive, seasonal naive and simple exponential smoothing
md: A parameter fitted to minimize one-step in-sample error is not automatically good at the horizon you care about. Always evaluate at the real horizon on data the fit never saw.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Chains and roots: how a browser validates a certificate
md: Trust flows down from the trust store, never up from the server. Everything the server sends is just a candidate until a signature path connects it to a root you already had.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Fused softmax: one row per program, reductions on chip
md: This design assumes a whole row fits in one block; the tutorial targets matrices whose rows fit in on-chip memory. For very long rows you would loop over chunks of the row inside the program and combine partial maxima and sums instead.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: One encoder or two: why Janus splits seeing from drawing
md: Shared vs separate encoders is a trade between simplicity and specialization. One encoder means one token type and one path, but semantic and reconstruction goals pull against each other. Two encoders let each path pick its best tool while the transformer still sees one sequence.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Concurrency in one address space: cooperative threads and no fork
md: Cooperative scheduling has no time slices. Any loop that neither waits nor yields holds the only vCPU until it ends, starving every other request and timer in the unikernel.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
md: A common mistake is to benchmark a distance kernel on a few thousand vectors that fit in L2 cache and extrapolate to a 100 GB index. The small benchmark measures compute; the real index measures memory.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Segments: immutable indexes, a write buffer, tombstones and merges
md: Immutable segments turn random in-place updates into sequential writes plus background rewrites. The price is read amplification: every query touches every segment, and dead rows cost time until a merge removes them.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Why verl splits the RL loop from the GPU programs
md: The controller decides **what runs and in what order**; each WorkerGroup decides **how** it runs on its GPUs. That is why a new algorithm is a change to one Python loop, and a new backend or placement is a change to the workers or the config, never both.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Why an hour of video does not fit: frames times tokens
md: Video cost is **frames x tokens per frame**. Every long-video method attacks one factor: fewer frames (sampling), fewer tokens per frame (pooling), fewer tokens over time (merging, memory), a bigger budget (long context), or a different representation (text captions).

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: The hypervisor as a security boundary: who must not reach whom
md: Misconception: "a VM is a sealed box, so an escape needs a CPU bug." Almost every escape in this course is ordinary software: a buffer overflow in an emulated floppy controller, a race in a virtual network card, an unchecked pointer in a virtual switch. The boundary is made of code, and it is large.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Case: Hyper-V's vmswitch, and how to read a hypervisor advisory
md: Do not triage by product name. "Hyper-V" in a title does not mean guest-to-host, and a 9.9 with "Exploitation Less Likely" (CVE-2021-28476) may be less urgent today than a 7.8 that is already exploited (CVE-2025-21333). Read the impact text, the scope, and the KEV status together.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
md: Preprocessing must match the checkpoint. `google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k` normalizes with mean 0.5 and std 0.5 per channel, while many timm ImageNet models use mean (0.485, 0.456, 0.406). Load the checkpoint's own settings (`AutoImageProcessor` in Transformers, `resolve_data_config` in timm) instead of copying numbers from another model.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Running action chunks in the control loop
md: Temporal ensembling is not a universal upgrade. The pi0 authors tried it early and found it hurt performance, so pi0 executes chunks open-loop: 16 actions then replan on 20 Hz robots (every 0.8 s), 25 actions on 50 Hz robots (every 0.5 s).

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation
md: Older guides set the `VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND` environment variable. It existed in `vllm/envs.py` up to the v0.14 release and is gone from main. Use `--attention-backend` or `--attention-config` (`-ac`). `AttentionConfig.backend_per_kind` can also set a backend per KV cache group kind, for example a different one for sliding-window MLA layers.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Hybrid models and KV cache groups: one pool, many block tables
md: A sliding-window group's block table is full of null entries. A backend that ignores the window and reads every position up to `seq_lens` will read block 0, which holds nothing meaningful. Supporting `supports_sliding_window` means honoring the window in the kernel, not just accepting the argument.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: What an image costs: provider token formulas and resizing rules
md: Resizing is silent by default. If your receipt is downscaled, small digits may become unreadable and any coordinates the model returns refer to the resized image. Anthropic's docs recommend resizing yourself first; OpenAI's guide notes images may be resized even with original detail.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
md: The template for almost every wait-free algorithm since: **announce** your operation in a per-thread slot, then **help** pending operations in an order that guarantees each announced operation gets its turn within a bounded number of steps.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
md: Every global score is an area-weighted average. Weights proportional to cos(latitude) count each unit of Earth's surface once.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authentication: enumeration, lockout, reset and skipped steps
md: Lockout and reset tests act on accounts. Run them only on accounts you created. A lockout test against a real user's account is a denial of service against that person.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Writing a report that gets triaged, fixed and paid
md: Write for three readers: the triager reproduces, the engineer fixes, the lead prioritises. Exact steps with your own accounts, evidence, plausible impact, reasoned severity, a suggested fix, and no one else's data.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Content Security Policy: telling the browser which scripts to trust
md: CSP is defence in depth, not a fix. A permissive policy with `'unsafe-inline'` stops almost nothing, and even a strict policy cannot help if your own trusted script takes attacker text and passes it to `eval()` or builds script elements from it. Encode output and validate input first; then add CSP.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Access tokens and the access check: how Windows says yes or no
md: Because the walk stops early, ACE order changes the result. Windows tools keep a canonical order: explicit denies, then explicit allows, then inherited denies, then inherited allows. Hand-built DACLs in the wrong order can grant access you meant to deny.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why a captured handshake allows offline password guessing
md: Changing the passphrase does not protect recordings already made: if an old passphrase is later guessed, every handshake recorded under it can be replayed into the PTK computation. With WPA2-Personal, the passphrase protects the past as well as the future.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app networking: cleartext, certificate checks and pinning
md: Leave certificate validation to the platform. The bug is almost always code that disables it: an empty trust manager, an always-true hostname verifier, a delegate that trusts any server, or a blanket ATS or cleartext exception. Pin only endpoints you control, and always ship a backup pin. Pins outlive app releases: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve keys after 2030, so plan rotation to post-quantum keys.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Why cosine forces you to fix the training length up front
md: Cosine couples the **shape** of the LR curve to the **end date** of training. You must choose the training length before you start, and every checkpoint before the end is half-annealed.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: sendfile: from the page cache straight to the socket
md: sendfile shares page cache pages with the network stack. The man page warns that the transferred part of the file must stay unmodified until the reader on the other end has consumed it. If another process rewrites the file mid-send, the bytes on the wire can be a mix of old and new.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
md: Two details. First, the bars show W p renormalized to sum to 1 for readability; the paper writes softmax(W p + b), which gives different numbers (T2 sports 0.911) but the same argmax, and the paper predicts with the argmax. Second, the bias is contextual: change the instruction, the examples, or their order, and p_cf must be measured again.
